title: Working Scientifically
seo_title: Year 8 Science: Working Scientifically Worksheets (Australian Curriculum)
standard_code: AC9S8I01, AC9S8I02, AC9S8I03, AC9S8I04, AC9S8I05, AC9S8I06
standard_text: Develop investigable questions and hypotheses; plan and conduct safe, valid investigations controlling variables; analyse data to identify relationships and anomalies; evaluate claims and methods; and use models and representations (summary of the Australian Curriculum v9.0 Year 8 science inquiry content descriptions).
meta_desc: Free Year 8 science worksheets on working scientifically: variables and controls, relationships in data, interpolation and extrapolation, evaluating claims, correlation and cause, and models. 100 questions with answers.
key_sub: Look for a fair test, a large sample, a control group and no bias before trusting a claim.
body_html:
How to think about it

Good science needs fair tests and careful thinking about data.

  • Change one independent variable, measure the dependent variable, and control the rest. Use a control group to compare.
  • Describe relationships from tables and graphs; interpolate between points, and be careful extrapolating beyond them.
  • Evaluate claims: Is the sample large? Is there a control? Who paid for it? Could something else cause the pattern?
Example

Mass 10, 20, 30 g; stretch 4, 8, 12 cm. Stretch for 25 g?

each 10 g adds 4 cm

25 g → 10 cm

Answer: 10 cm

Example

Ice-cream sales and drownings both rise in summer. Cause?

both rise with hot weather

Answer: no; correlation is not cause

Common mistakes

  • Thinking a correlation proves cause.
  • Trusting a claim from a tiny sample or with no control group.
  • Extrapolating far beyond the range of the data.

faq.q: What is the difference between interpolation and extrapolation?
faq.a: Interpolation estimates a value between data points you measured. Extrapolation extends the pattern beyond your data, which is less reliable.

faq.q: How do I evaluate a claim?
faq.a: Ask whether it was a fair test with a control, whether the sample was large and representative, who paid for the study, and whether something else could explain the result.

faq.q: Why are models useful if they are not perfect?
faq.a: Models help explain and predict things that are hard to see, such as particles or the solar system. Scientists improve models when new evidence appears.

items.q: Which graph is best to show how plant height changes over 6 weeks?
c: a pie chart
a line graph
no graph
a column graph of plant names
items.e: Use a line graph for continuous data over time.

items.q: Mia tests whether the colour of a car affects how hot it gets inside. Which question is testable?
c: Which car colour is best?
Does the colour of a car affect the temperature inside after 1 hour in the sun?
Why do people buy white cars?
Are black cars nicer?
items.e: A testable question names the variables.

items.q: What is a limitation of a ball-and-stick model of a molecule?
c: Real atoms are not solid balls and bonds are not sticks.
It has no limitations.
It is too accurate.
It shows too many atoms.
items.e: Models simplify reality.

items.q: Why should a sample be random?
c: so the test is quicker
so it is smaller
so it represents the whole group without bias
so the results are the same
items.e: Choosing only some people can bias results.

items.q: Jack's results: one trial is much higher than the rest. What should he do first?
c: include it without checking
delete all his data
check for a mistake and repeat that trial
change his hypothesis
items.e: Anomalies should be checked.

items.q: Why should criteria be precise, like “hold 2 kg” instead of “be strong”?
c: Precise criteria can be measured to see if a design succeeds.
It does not matter.
Vague criteria are always better.
Precise criteria are shorter.
items.e: You can test a measurable criterion.

items.q: Aarav repeats his test five times and gets almost the same answer each time. What does this show?
c: His results must be accurate.
His hypothesis is wrong.
His results are repeatable (precise).
He changed the variable.
items.e: Repeatable results may still have a systematic error.

items.q: A class investigates how the length of a pendulum affects the time for 10 swings. Which variables should be controlled (kept the same)?
c: the time for 10 swings
the same drop height and the same load
the same mass and the same starting angle
the length of the pendulum
items.e: Change: the length of the pendulum. Measure: the time for 10 swings. Keep the same: the same mass and the same starting angle.

items.q: Which graph is best to compare the number of each type of bird seen in a park?
c: a pie chart of temperatures
a column graph
a line graph
a scatter plot
items.e: Categories suit a column graph.

items.q: What is the independent variable?
c: the variable you change on purpose
the result
the variable you measure
the variables you keep the same
items.e: It goes on the x-axis.

items.q: A class investigates how the height of a ramp affects how far a toy car rolls. Which variables should be controlled (kept the same)?
c: the same drop height and the same load
the same car and the same floor surface
how far the car rolls
the height of the ramp
items.e: Change: the height of the ramp. Measure: how far the car rolls. Keep the same: the same car and the same floor surface.

items.q: Kai's team is designing a water filter for a camping trip. Which is a criterion (what the design must do)?
c: It must cost less than $10.
It must weigh less than 500 g.
It must be finished by Friday.
It must filter 1 litre in under 5 minutes.
items.e: Criteria describe what a successful solution must do.

items.q: Why might a design need to consider effects on the environment?
c: Solutions can cause new problems for people and nature.
Only to make it look good.
The environment never matters.
It makes the design cheaper always.
items.e: Good designs limit harmful effects.

items.q: A class investigates how the type of surface affects how far a marble rolls. Which is the independent variable (the one you change)?
c: the number of batteries
the same marble and the same push

the type of surface
items.e: Change: the type of surface. Measure: the distance the marble rolls. Keep the same: the same marble and the same push.

items.q: A class investigates how the length of a pendulum affects the time for 10 swings. Which is the independent variable (the one you change)?

items.e: Change: the length of the pendulum. Measure: the time for 10 swings. Keep the same: the same mass and the same starting angle.

items.q: In a fair test of two designs, what should stay the same?
c: only the colour
nothing
the design being tested

items.e: Only the design should differ.

items.q: Noah's experiment gives results that agree closely, but his ruler was missing the first 1 cm. What kind of error is this?
c: an anomaly
a random error
no error
a systematic error
items.e: Every reading is shifted by the same amount.

items.q: A friend says rain always comes after his footy team wins, because it happened twice. What is the main problem with this claim?
c: Nothing is wrong; one result is enough.
Two events are not enough data, and there is no reason one causes the other.
The claim is wrong because the scientists were young.
The claim is proven because it was published online.
items.e: Good evidence needs a fair test, a large sample, a control and no bias.

items.q: Kai uses a data logger instead of a stopwatch. How does this improve his investigation?
c: It changes the independent variable.
It makes the test unfair.
It removes the need for a hypothesis.
It reduces human reaction-time error and records more readings.
items.e: Better equipment improves accuracy.

to explain and predict things that are too small, big or complex to see directly
to make science harder
items.e: Every model has limitations.

items.e: Large, long-term data sets make trends reliable.
